Common Ground

How Common Ground built Lïef Development's brand and site

One company with two audiences became two brands with a written rule for which to use, and a company site that search and AI engines can read.

Lïef Development had one company and two audiences. Investors, developers, general contractors and trade press needed to see a builder with a deep bench. Home buyers and design press needed to see a place to live. One identity could not speak to both, and in early 2026 the company site had been generated in an AI site builder and could not be read well by search or AI engines.

Common Ground's decision was to split Lïef into a company brand and a project brand with a written rule for which one to use, and to treat the company site as a record that machines can read as well as a page people look at. The brand system was a team effort across the principals.

What Common Ground did

  • Set the company identity: a deep green, a neon green accent held to 10 to 15 percent of any layout, Archivo Black for headlines and DM Sans for body text. The neon accent never fills a background.
  • Defined the two-brand architecture. Lïef Development is the company brand. Lïef Osborn, the project brand, speaks to home buyers in warm earth tones set in Japandi. A decision table assigns each kind of content to one system, and the two are never blended in a single asset.
  • Wrote the spelling rule: the name carries the diaeresis in all brand copy and drops it only in domains, email addresses and handles.
  • Put the search and AI readiness layer on anewlief.com between March 10 and July 17, 2026: structured data, AI crawler rules, a plain-text fact sheet for AI engines, the spelling of Lïef, and rewrites of the FAQ and positioning copy. On July 17, 2026 every route was written out as a static page with its own canonical address.
  • Planned a 13-week LinkedIn program for March 31 to June 27, 2026: one carousel and two image posts a week, 39 pieces, across five content pillars. Only a handful of the 39 were published, and the carousel template system was retired on April 20, 2026 in favor of a principle-driven approach.
  • Wrote the company fact sheet for the media kit in May 2025 and produced Lïef tiles for the email signatures of five principals in July 2026.
  • Jesse Fowler supplied the name Lïef and the narrative the brand is built around, contributed to the company site, and is the primary voice for the company on LinkedIn.

What came of it

  • Both Lïef company sites are live, and the older company domain redirects to anewlief.com.
  • An outside marketing agency reviewed the two-brand system in April 2026 and called the split "one of the smarter structural decisions we've seen in a project brief."
  • An internal audit on July 17, 2026 graded anewlief.com C minus and named the pattern from the Lïef Midtown site as the fix. The commit that applied that pattern to the code landed the same day.
  • The standard was unified into one two-system document on May 2, 2026 and is marked active, with both palettes and both type pairings locked.

About Common Ground

Common Ground is a principal-led venture group built around one premise: we build. It builds, funds, operates, automates with AI and protects companies from the inside, and it carries the work from strategy through execution instead of stopping at the recommendation.

The group works across related industries on purpose. Construction, capital, brand, technology and law sit in one room, so a developer's problem can borrow from a product launch, and a deep tech company's sales plan can borrow from how a builder wins a bid. Every engagement is a chance to carry what worked somewhere else into the next company.

Common Ground grew out of two practices: Jesse Fowler's fractional work, running since 2016 and as Three Trails since 2019, and Lip Loi Creative, since December 2019. The principals brought them together as Common Ground in April 2023, when Alex Prince and Prince Capital came in as well. Zen Aegis came in the same way in December 2025.
